title: Minerva 26 CEO Kelly Twigger on Leading E-Discovery into the AI Age
author: Kelly Twigger

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source contains only podcast closing remarks and offers no substantive claim, evidence or recommendation about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation or transformation. Its position relative to the cluster proposition therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source accepts technology-enabled legal delivery and materially extends the cluster’s implementation account by recommending planning around recurring cases, data and clients’ internal expertise. Its Percipient segment also illustrates integrated professional, technology and project-management delivery, but only as an unverified promotional claim rather than evidence of realised savings or strategic capacity.
qs: But if you just get a plan for the cases that you handle, the types of data that you see on a regular basis and work directly with your clients and whatever expertise they already have to do that internally, you can do it a lot more effectively.
Our team of legal professionals leverage tech and project management principles with the right amount of human oversight to deliver precise, efficient, and cost-effective legal solutions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Twigger accepts the cluster’s selective, human-led deployment model and extends it with concrete e-discovery operating evidence: AI summaries require recurring sampled verification and prompt refinement, while current systems remain constrained by limited back-end capacity. Her account also illustrates work reallocation through leaner review teams rather than comprehensive autonomy.
qs: But every week, I get a report from my team of random generated 50 summaries from cases, and I read them and I go, well, we need to tweak this a little bit or we need to do this.
Especially in E-Discovery when you actually talk about the E-Discovery work, because the back-end tech, it's just not there to process the volumes of information that E-Discovery software does today.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI pressures delivery economics and may sharply reduce review-team staffing, while reinforcing that these effects remain early and predictive rather than established. Its suggestion that pricing may remain unchanged also aligns with the cluster’s view that efficiency does not dictate a single pricing outcome. It does not materially address apprenticeship, verification or end-to-end redesign.
qs: I think it's probably going to be subject matter expert and a couple of reviewers are going to get the job done.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Twigger supports the cluster’s cautious, lawyer-guided framing by describing targeted AI uses and planned human involvement while stressing that current systems cannot process full e-discovery volumes. Her practitioner observations reinforce the distinction between useful assistance and dependable end-to-end performance, without providing measured results.
qs: We also are creating a human in the loop series.
Especially in E-Discovery when you actually talk about the E-Discovery work, because the back-end tech, it's just not there to process the volumes of information that E-Discovery software does today.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Twigger directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI is reshaping technology-enabled legal production—especially document review—by reducing labour requirements and improving efficiency, while augmenting rather than replacing lawyers. Her emphasis on early-stage adoption, education and system interoperability also aligns with the cluster’s cautions about organisational absorption.
qs: I'm not one of those people who ascribes to the notion that AI is going to replace lawyers.
I think it's probably going to be subject matter expert and a couple of reviewers are going to get the job done.

kp.k: Electronic evidence enables leaner, faster litigation analysis
kp.d: Twigger describes ESI Attorneys as a largely solo practice that scales with contractors and technology rather than permanent overhead. She attributes faster fact finding, early claim assessment and integrated timelines to electronic evidence and improved tools, not solely to generative AI. Her comparisons with paper-based work are practitioner observations, not measured productivity findings.
qs: But I don't keep a lot of employees on, I don't keep a lot of overhead.
With ESI, I can make five calls, have all the technology I need in minutes to be able to deal with data, and I can do way more than you could ever do with a staff of like 10 people.
That visualization of data is something that we never could have with paper.

kp.k: Early discovery strategy preserves analytical options and reduces costs
kp.d: Twigger recommends addressing preservation, retention, third-party subpoenas, ESI protocols and production formats early. She argues that delayed involvement raises costs and reduces the usefulness of evidence, particularly when missing metadata prevents later filtering and analysis. These are recommendations grounded in her practice experience rather than quantified savings.
qs: But the later you start in E-Discovery, the more it will cost you and the less you're going to get out of the information that you get.
So when you don't ask for the right metadata fields from a particular source of ESI, whether it's social media or Teams or Slack or anything, you lose the ability to filter on specific types of data.
If you've got third-party subpoenas, you need to send those out now because they're going to take months to get through when you've got a shortened schedule.

kp.k: Fear, expense and limited learning time impede adoption
kp.d: Twigger identifies fear of technology, discovery and not personally reviewing everything as obstacles, alongside expense and data complexity. She recommends repeatable plans tailored to common matters, collaboration with clients' existing expertise and education, while acknowledging that lawyers lack time for the frequent targeted learning rapid technological change would require.
qs: I think that it's fear and it's expense, right?
Fear of e-discovery generally, fear of technology, fear of not looking at everything.
You almost need to be doing an hour a week of somebody giving you really targeted education on what's happening this week.
And that's not going to happen. We lawyers have too much to do as it is.

kp.k: Discovery economics can conflict with technology-enabled efficiency
kp.d: Twigger contrasts an older discovery business model built on more data and client expenditure with economical delivery using appropriate technology and knowledge. She questions whether service providers will embrace AI-driven review changes or prioritize existing earnings; this is a concern about incentives, not evidence that all providers resist change.
qs: One of the initial reasons that I started ESI Attorneys in 2009 was because the business model of E-Discovery was, let's have more and more and more data and spend more and more and more of the client's money and the most effective way to do E-Discovery is to do it economically and efficiently with the right technology and the right knowledge.
And are the people who were providing services in that area willing to adapt to those changes and embrace them? Or do they just want to make as much money as they can?

kp.k: Host predicts substantially smaller document-review teams
kp.d: Host Chad Main, rather than Twigger, suggests existing tools have reduced illustrative review staffing from 50 people to probably 15 and predicts AI could leave a subject-matter expert and a couple of reviewers doing the work. He says pricing might not need to change and describes his company as exploring tools. Both speakers characterize the transition as early; the staffing figures are not presented as study results.
qs: But so, I mean, it's early days, real early days.
It's going to change where you needed, back in the day, you needed 50 people. Now you probably need 15 because the tools you can use in the front end to do it.
I think it's probably going to be subject matter expert and a couple of reviewers are going to get the job done.
The pricing might not have to change.

kp.k: Twigger expects augmentation and changing support roles
kp.d: Twigger rejects the proposition that AI will replace lawyers, instead expecting improvements in work quality and speed. She reports declining administrative support over the last five to ten years and expects further decline, but argues that disconnected software systems still require support. She anticipates assistants, paralegals and legal assistants needing greater technological competence.
qs: I'm not one of those people who ascribes to the notion that AI is going to replace lawyers.
And that is, it will improve a lot of the things that you either weren't doing or you could do better, faster, stronger.
And we've already seen a huge down tick in the amount of administrative support that law firms have over the last five, ten years. And I think that's going to increase.
Or the assistance, the paralegals, the legal assistants are going to need to become more educated on the technology and how that enhances the law firm's capabilities.

kp.k: Firm incentives and client constraints slow organizational change
kp.d: Twigger reports hearing in-house counsel criticize outside counsel's discovery capabilities, while emphasizing that both sides face time constraints. She attributes firms' underinvestment partly to pressure to earn revenue and service clients, rather than deliberate rejection of competence. She sees hiring chief innovation officers as a developing route to business-led improvement.
qs: I mean, I talked to many, many in-house counsel who say our outside counsel are abysmal at E-Discovery, and we know they're abysmal.

They are caught in a loop of must make money, must keep servicing clients, and it's hard to step back in the law and say, if I invest 20 to 40 hours or $50,000 here, I'm going to reap that going forward.
We're seeing a lot of law firms that are retaining Chief Innovation Officers, and those are people that we talk to for use of Minerva.

kp.k: Specialized platforms combine knowledge, consulting and practical training
kp.d: Twigger distinguishes Minerva 26's discovery-strategy knowledge platform from tools that process evidence. It curates case law, issue tags, rules and practice materials; she claims targeted research takes minutes rather than hours. Minerva also provides technology-design, implementation and training consulting, while legal consulting remains at ESI Attorneys. Training includes one- and two-day programs, limited to 10 to 15 participants a day, using hypotheticals, interviews and meet-and-confers; an on-demand equivalent was planned for July under a separate subscription.
qs: So where you've got tools to handle data, this is a tool for your knowledge, for your E-Discovery strategy.
So, what would take you hours to find in a larger research database that has all the content in it, now takes you just a few minutes to get to the decisions you actually want to review.
So legal-based consulting, I do at the law firm, if you need the legal piece of it.
We have to limit it to 10 to 15 folks a day.
You're not just listening to me talk.

kp.k: Current generative AI use centers on content and summaries
kp.d: Twigger reports using AI for writing, marketing, improving training transcripts and summarizing the platform's 40-some thousand decisions. She says current use is mostly on the Minerva side and excludes the ESI side under the system she describes as 'open source'; she would use a closed-loop system there. The transcript does not further define those deployment terms.
qs: Of course, we don't use it on the ESI side because it's open source, right? If we have a closed loop system that we can use, then we'll use that.
So we use it mostly on the Minerva 26 side.
Actually, we have it plugged in to summarize every single one of the 40-some thousand decisions that we have in the E-Discovery database.
I also use it to improve any of the learning and the training transcripts that I have.

kp.k: Planned curation automation retains human review and feedback
kp.d: Twigger describes existing case selection, issue tagging and links to relevant rules as highly manual. Minerva is building a human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI performs the first pass, humans continue reviewing and their input feeds back into training. She attributes feasibility to recent improvements in reasoning capabilities; this is a development plan, not an evaluated deployment.
qs: Our team does that a lot right now. It's very manual and so what we're building is, because the reasoning capabilities of AI have improved so much over the last year, we're building what's called a human-in-the-loop system.
So the AI will be able to take a first pass at it and then the human will continue their review and be able, whatever information the human provides, it will go back into the training loop.

kp.k: Ask Minerva would connect questions to curated legal resources
kp.d: Twigger describes a planned retrieval-augmented question interface, Ask Minerva, using what she calls a fine-tuned instance of RAG. It would answer questions, link users to supporting platform information and execute issue-tag searches. She identifies Q4 as the implementation target in this 2025 interview; no performance results are provided.
qs: The other thing that we're building at Minerva is taking that same reasoning capability and creating a fine-tuned instance of rag to be able to create what we'll call Ask Minerva.
It will give you a response and it will also link you to all the information within the Minerva 26 tool that you need to take a look at.
So that's what we're working on building because that technology is advancing and that's like a Q4 implementation for us.

kp.k: AI summaries require continuing human checks and prompt revision
kp.d: Twigger cautions that summaries omit desired information. She reports introducing Minerva's summaries in September 2023, revising the prompt probably four times and personally reading a weekly report of 50 randomly generated case summaries to identify further changes. This is an operational quality-checking account, not a measured error rate. She says newer reasoning models produce better summaries but disclaims knowledge of other discovery platforms' backend processes.
qs: It doesn't get everything that you want it to get.
Let's see, we introduced that in September 2023.
we've re-engineered that prompt probably four times to be more clear, more consistent.
But every week, I get a report from my team of random generated 50 summaries from cases, and I read them and I go, well, we need to tweak this a little bit or we need to do this.
So it's not a quit it and forget it kind of situation

kp.k: AI promise exceeds current discovery capabilities
kp.d: Twigger says AI discussion exceeds available capabilities. Main specifically argues that backend AI technology cannot yet process the volumes handled by current discovery software, with Twigger agreeing; neither provides a timetable or benchmark. Twigger identifies existing uses in contract lifecycle management and litigation summarization, while explicitly qualifying her knowledge of individual vendors' features and noting that summarization may carry additional charges.
qs: There's a lot more talk about AI than there are capabilities.
Especially in E-Discovery when you actually talk about the E-Discovery work, because the back-end tech, it's just not there to process the volumes of information that E-Discovery software does today.
I would agree with that.
I don't know what all the platforms capabilities are there.

kp.k: Lawyers must supply courts with accurate technical explanations
kp.d: Twigger distinguishes judges' greater familiarity with discovery issues from uneven understanding of underlying technology. She places responsibility on lawyers to explain technical facts and support proportionality arguments, citing her reading of hyperlink-file decisions and cookie-discovery disputes. Her observations are qualitative, not a systematic assessment of judicial knowledge.
qs: I think that the bench is infinitely more knowledgeable about e-discovery issues now than they were ten years ago.
It's the lawyer's job to explain to the judge what they need to know for the outcome of whatever they're bringing to them.
what the parties tell the court becomes part of the record. And sometimes it's not accurate.
And I see a lot in the case law of just sort of spurious arguments, throwing proportionality at the wall to see if it'll stick with no underlying facts about why something isn't proportional.

kp.k: Changing evidence sources prompt calls for procedural-rule reform
kp.d: Twigger argues that collaboration platforms, hyperlinked files and work communications on personal phones have outpaced legal knowledge and existing discovery frameworks. She reports conflicting judicial approaches to employer control of employees' personal phones under Rule 34 and calls for rule changes. She also identifies judicial time, expertise and budget constraints as implementation obstacles.
qs: I think we need some updates to the rules.

In particular, we've got judges across the country who are completely split on, does an employer have control of an employee's personal phone if they use it for work-related information that is clearly relevant to the context of the litigation.
Then we've got other judges that are relying on the legal right and the practical ability test under possession, custody or control under Rule 34.
There are a lot of outside forces that are impacting, cuts in budgets are impacting.

kp.k: AI increases pressure to clarify review-method transparency
kp.d: Twigger argues users should be prepared to explain AI tools to courts or opposing parties. She points to continuing disputes over disclosure of technology-assisted review as evidence of procedural ambiguity, expresses the view that Rule 34 does not generally require disclosure of how production obligations are met, and describes successful arguments for greater transparency when supported by specific facts. She recommends clearer federal rules informed by technical expertise and balanced between plaintiffs and defendants.
qs: I think there's exponential capabilities, but I also think if you're using them, you have to be prepared to explain how they work to a court or to the other side.
We're still having fights about whether if I choose to do TAR, I have to disclose that to you.
I've had success as an expert with some folks arguing that there needs to be more transparency in the TAR process, but with a factual basis that necessitated it.
My point is that with all this development in technology and the use of AI, we're going to have to have a bit more clarity in the federal rules.
And then we've got to make sure they benefit both defendants and plaintiffs.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kelly Twigger describes AI as augmenting lawyers, changing document review and support work, and enabling partially automated legal-knowledge workflows, while requiring continuing human oversight and clearer procedural rules.
pts.d: Twigger rejects the prediction that AI will replace lawyers; instead, she says it improves work lawyers could perform better or were not previously doing. She says AI is already changing document review, while questioning how quickly service providers will adapt rather than preserve existing revenues. She predicts that the decline in law-firm administrative support will continue, but that support remains necessary because disconnected software systems require data organisation and coordination; assistants and paralegals will need greater technological knowledge. At Minerva 26, she reports current AI use for writing, marketing, training transcripts and summaries of its roughly 40,000-plus decisions. She describes a planned human-in-the-loop system in which AI first assesses and tags incoming case law, humans review it, and their input feeds further training. She also describes Ask Minerva, a planned retrieval-augmented question-answering interface that will answer questions and link users to relevant platform information. She identifies contract lifecycle management and litigation summarisation as useful applications, but says summaries omit information and require ongoing attention. Finally, she argues that AI and related discovery technologies increase the need for clarity in federal procedural rules, particularly around disclosure and transparency of review methods. The host's numerical forecast of shrinking review teams is not attributed to Twigger.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily Twigger's professional experience, daily AI use and internal product-development and summary-review practices, rather than comparative studies or formal benchmarks.
pts.d: Twigger grounds her augmentation claim in her own daily AI use and her support-role prediction in an observed decline in administrative staffing. She offers operational examples from Minerva 26: AI summarisation across tens of thousands of decisions, approximately four prompt revisions since introducing summaries in September 2023, and weekly review of 50 randomly generated summaries supplied by her team. These illustrate her basis for saying that summaries improve with newer reasoning models but still miss information; she supplies no measured accuracy or omission rate. Her claims about improving reasoning capabilities and future automation rely on development experience and expectations, with no benchmark results presented. The proposed case-law workflow and Ask Minerva are described as projects under construction, not demonstrated outcomes. Her call for procedural clarity draws on experience with disputes over technology-assisted review and expert work seeking greater transparency where supported by facts; these are not AI performance tests. Her comments on third-party platforms are qualified by acknowledged limits to her knowledge of their capabilities and internal summarisation processes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Twigger distinguishes existing uses from near-term product plans and open-ended changes, with adoption constrained by education, fear, confidentiality-related system choices, cost and continuing human review.
pts.d: At the 2025 interview, Twigger describes review-market change and writing and summarisation uses as already occurring. She characterises reasoning capabilities as having improved over the preceding year, particularly six months, and anticipates further improvement over the next six months without quantifying it. Ask Minerva is targeted for Q4, implicitly Q4 2025; no precise launch date is given for the human-in-the-loop ingestion workflow. Continued reductions and changes in administrative support have no explicit forecast horizon. Twigger agrees that AI adoption is at an early stage and identifies fear of technology and of not examining everything as barriers. She sees education as necessary but difficult to fit into lawyers' schedules. Her current use is mostly on the Minerva side: she says she does not use the system she calls 'open source' on the ESI legal-practice side, while indicating willingness to use a 'closed loop system.' These are her terms, not a technical specification of deployment or licensing. Litigation summarisation is conditional on willingness to pay, and effective reliance requires ongoing checking and adjustment rather than unattended use. She warns that capabilities lag discussion and says users should be prepared to explain tools to courts or opposing parties. Rule reform is a recommendation, not an enacted change or a dated forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practising lawyers, discovery-review providers, law-firm support staff, legal-technology teams and users, and litigants and courts.
pts.d: Lawyers are positioned as beneficiaries of better and faster work rather than wholesale replacement, but face learning and explanation responsibilities. Discovery-review service providers face pressure to adapt their delivery practices and commercial incentives; Twigger does not quantify staffing reductions or predict a particular pricing model. Administrative assistants, legal assistants and paralegals face reduced aggregate support staffing and a shift toward more technologically informed roles, while system-coordination work remains necessary. Minerva's internal team would move from highly manual case selection and tagging toward reviewing AI first passes, and platform users would gain AI-assisted answers and links to relevant legal materials. Law firms and in-house departments using contract lifecycle management or litigation tools are potential users of the applications she discusses, subject to tool capabilities and cost. Litigating parties and judges face questions about how AI-enabled review works and what must be disclosed; Twigger says rule changes should benefit both plaintiffs and defendants. Minerva is discussed as a software, education and consulting business, distinct from ESI Attorneys' legal practice; the interview does not establish an AI-driven shift to an ALSP delivery model or make an access-to-justice claim.
